flashcardContentBlock.content: What is a sufficient condition in conditional logic?
A condition that is enough on its own to guarantee an outcome (the trigger).
What is a necessary condition in conditional logic?
A condition that is strictly required for an outcome to occur (the requirement).
In the conditional statement "If $A$, then $B$", which variable represents the sufficient condition?
$A$ (the condition attached to "if" on the left side of the arrow).
In the conditional statement "If $A$, then $B$", which variable represents the necessary condition?
$B$ (the outcome on the right side of the arrow).
When visualizing a conditional statement with concentric circles, where is the sufficient condition placed?
In the smaller inner circle contained entirely within the larger necessary condition circle.
What does the directional arrow in a conditional diagram ($A \rightarrow B$) signify?
A one-way guarantee: if the left side ($A$) is true, the right side ($B$) must also be true.
What are Group 1 (left-side) conditional indicator words?
Keywords that introduce a sufficient condition, such as *if*, *when*, *whenever*, *all*, *every*, *each*, and *any*.
What are Group 2 (right-side) conditional indicator words?
Keywords that introduce a necessary condition, such as *only if*, *requires*, *must*, *prerequisite*, and *only*.
How does the conditional indicator "only if" differ from "if"?
"If" introduces a sufficient condition (left side), whereas "only if" introduces a necessary condition (right side).
What valid inference can be made when you learn that a sufficient condition is met?
You can conclude that the necessary condition must also be true.
What valid inference can be made when you learn that a necessary condition is NOT met?
You can conclude that the sufficient condition is also not true (the contrapositive).
What is a contrapositive?
A logically equivalent restatement of a conditional that flips the order and negates both conditions ($\text{not } B \rightarrow \text{not } A$).
What invalid inference occurs when you infer the left side is true because the right side is true?
Reversing the conditional (affirming the necessary condition).
What invalid inference occurs when you infer the right side is false because the left side is false?
Inverting the conditional (denying the sufficient condition).
What logical flaw is committed when an argument treats a necessary condition as if it were sufficient?
Confusing necessary and sufficient conditions.
Does learning that a sufficient condition is false allow you to conclude that the necessary condition is false?
No; when the trigger is false, the rule simply disappears and gives no information about the necessary condition.
How do you diagram statements quantified by "No" (e.g., "No $A$s are $B$s")?
Place the subject on the left and negate the second term on the right ($A \rightarrow \text{not } B$).
What is the "if not" translation method for the word "unless"?
Replace "unless" with "if not" and place the attached idea, negated, on the left side of the arrow.
What is the "requirement" translation method for the word "unless"?
Place the idea following "unless" directly on the right side as a necessary condition, and negate the remaining idea on the left.
Which keywords follow the exact same translation rules as "unless"?
*Until* and *without*.
How does the word "and" transform when taking the contrapositive of a conditional rule?
"And" transforms into "or".
How does the word "or" transform when taking the contrapositive of a conditional rule?
"Or" transforms into "and".
What is the contrapositive of $A \text{ and } B \rightarrow C$?
$\text{not } C \rightarrow \text{not } A \text{ or } \text{not } B$.
What is the contrapositive of $X \rightarrow Y \text{ or } \text{not } Z$?
$\text{not } Y \text{ and } Z \rightarrow \text{not } X$.
What is a biconditional statement?
A conditional relationship that flows in both directions, indicated by phrases like "if and only if" ($A \leftrightarrow B$).
What two scenarios are possible under the biconditional statement $A \leftrightarrow B$?

1. Both $A$ and $B$ occur.
2. Neither $A$ nor $B$ occurs.
How can the word "otherwise" create a biconditional statement?
By providing a second condition that is the explicit logical opposite of the first rule.
What structural condition is required to chain two conditional statements together?
The necessary condition of one statement must match the sufficient condition of the other.
Given the chain $A \rightarrow B \rightarrow C \rightarrow D$, what main conclusion can be inferred?
$A \rightarrow D$ (and its contrapositive $\text{not } D \rightarrow \text{not } A$).
What is the subset visual model for understanding conditionals?
Visualizing the sufficient condition as a smaller subset category within a broader necessary condition category.
What is the partial list of requirements model for understanding conditionals?
Visualizing the necessary condition as one known ingredient required for a goal, alongside potentially other unknown requirements.
What is the "one of many paths" model for understanding conditionals?
Visualizing the sufficient condition as one specific path that leads to a destination (necessary condition), among other possible paths.
How does LSAT interpretation of a conditional statement differ from real-life interpretation?
The LSAT requires strict, literal interpretation without relying on conversational assumptions or unstated real-world context.
Diagram the statement: "Anyone in New York is in the USA."
$\text{New York} \rightarrow \text{USA}$.
Diagram the statement: "You must study hard if you want to get a great LSAT score."
$\text{Great LSAT Score} \rightarrow \text{Study Hard}$.
Diagram the statement: "Finishing in the top three guarantees winning a medal."
$\text{Top Three} \rightarrow \text{Medal}$.
Does the statement "Finishing in the top three guarantees winning a medal" mean that competitors outside the top three do not get medals?
No; top three guarantees a medal, but the statement leaves open the possibility that others might also receive medals.
Diagram the statement: "Eddie can't go to Legoland until he feeds his rabbit."
$\text{Legoland} \rightarrow \text{Feed Rabbit}$ (or $\text{Not Feed Rabbit} \rightarrow \text{Not Legoland}$).
Diagram the statement: "No camels attend law school."
$\text{Camel} \rightarrow \text{Not Law School}$ (or $\text{Law School} \rightarrow \text{Not Camel}$).
Diagram the statement: "Happiness is never achieved unless love or passion is present."
$\text{Happiness} \rightarrow \text{Love or Passion}$ (or $\text{Not Love and Not Passion} \rightarrow \text{Not Happiness}$).
How do you translate the negative quantifier "Few $A$s are $B$" into a positive translation?
Most $A$s are not $B$.
How do you translate the negative quantifier "Not all $A$s are $B$" into a positive translation?
Some $A$s are not $B$.
Given the rule $A \rightarrow B \text{ or } C$, and the facts that $A$ is true and $C$ is false, what fact can be inferred?
$B$ must be true.
Given the rules $A \text{ and } B \rightarrow C$, and $C \rightarrow D$, alongside the fact that $A$ is true, what additional fact is needed to guarantee $D$?
$B$ must be true.
What type of condition does the word "prerequisite" introduce?
A necessary condition (Group 2 word, placed on the right side of the arrow).
Diagram the statement: "Running requires that you've learned to walk."
$\text{Run} \rightarrow \text{Learn to Walk}$.
Diagram the statement: "Enjoying fudge implies enjoying sugar."
$\text{Enjoy Fudge} \rightarrow \text{Enjoy Sugar}$.
Diagram the statement: "Lou's golf balls are each covered in bird poop."
$\text{Lou's Golf Ball} \rightarrow \text{Bird Poop}$.
Diagram the statement: "Real men never shy away from a yogurt parfait."
$\text{Real Man} \rightarrow \text{Not Shy Away}$.
Diagram the statement: "Using breath strips instead of mints is done only by cool people."
$\text{Breath Strips} \rightarrow \text{Cool Person}$.
Diagram the statement: "Vanessa can't work without tea and snacks."
$\text{Work} \rightarrow \text{Tea and Snacks}$ (or $\text{Not Tea or Not Snacks} \rightarrow \text{Not Work}$).
Why is standard conditional diagramming supplemented with mental visual models?
Standard arrows do not visually explain why moving backward or negating both sides without flipping is invalid.
When is explicit conditional diagramming most useful during the LSAT?
When handling complex conditional chains, tricky indicator language (e.g., *unless*), or parallel reasoning questions.
Is a conditional statement logically equivalent to its contrapositive?
Yes; a conditional rule and its contrapositive express the exact same logical meaning.
What happens to a multi-step conditional chain ($A \rightarrow B \rightarrow C$) when taking its contrapositive?
The entire chain is reversed and every term is negated: $\text{not } C \rightarrow \text{not } B \rightarrow \text{not } A$.
What is the primary function of Group 1 conditional keywords?
To signal that the attached concept acts as the trigger or sufficient condition.
What is the primary function of Group 2 conditional keywords?
To signal that the attached concept acts as a requirement or necessary condition.
If performing an action out of self-interest means it should NOT be considered generous, does an action performed without self-interest prove it IS generous?
No; concluding that it is generous commits the invalid flaw of inverting the conditional.
In the statement "A sidewalk is open to the public only if it has no ice," which condition is necessary?
Having no ice on the sidewalk.
Diagram the statement: "Jeff takes a vacation if, but only if, Trixie gets a promotion."
$\text{Vacation} \leftrightarrow \text{Promotion}$.
